warmup.q: A flow cooks one dish every 100 ms and emits it. The collector, the diner, needs 300 ms to eat each dish. There is no buffer. When does the second emit happen?
options: At t=200 ms: the cook keeps cooking while the diner eats
At t=400 ms: right after the first dish is eaten
At t=500 ms: the first dish is eaten at 400, then the cook needs 100 ms more
At t=300 ms: the two sides overlap halfway
warmup.why: emit(1) is called at 100 ms and doesn't return until the diner has finished, at 400 ms. Only then does the cook start the next dish, which takes another 100 ms. The answer t=200 assumes emit drops the value into a queue, which a plain flow never does. The section on the three rules works it out on a virtual clock.

opening:
Picture the home cook from the coroutines track at dinner time. Tonight's recipe card lists three dishes: soup, salad and roast. The card cooks nothing by itself. When a diner sits down and asks to be served, the cook starts at the top. She makes the soup, carries the bowl to the table and stays there while the diner eats. This kitchen has no counter and no shelf, so there is nowhere to put a plate down. Only when the bowl is empty does she walk back and start the salad. It's lovely service, and it makes for a long dinner.

A Kotlin flow serves its values the same way. The easy trap is to picture emit dropping a value into a queue while the cook carries on.

The coroutines track ended with Coroutines meet Java, where flows crossed into Java and Reactor and back like sealed boxes. In this lesson, we'll open the box: predict a dinner's print order, build a flow from two small interfaces, read the stack from inside the diner, and trace the rules from Flow basics back to one function call. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook who carries each plate to the table and waits while the diner eats. A flow is that kitchen: two interfaces, a builder that only stores the recipe, and an emit that calls straight into the collector. Cold, one value at a time and backpressure all come from that one call, and so does the wait.

Now look in your own code for a timer or a log line wrapped around emit. It measures everything downstream, not the producer's own work.

Next, we'll meet the inspector that flow { } puts at the kitchen door. What does it check on every emit, and why does a try/catch around emit lose the rest of dinner?

sections.h: Predict the order: a cook, a diner and three dishes
sections.html:
Here is that dinner as a flow. A flow is a stream of values that a program hands over one at a time, and flow { } is the usual way to build one. Inside its block, emit(dish) hands one value to whoever is collecting. collect { } is the call that asks for the values: it runs the block and receives each one.

In this track the people in the kitchen get jobs in the code. The cook is the producer, the code inside flow { } that makes the values. The diner is the collector, the code inside collect { } that receives them.

The cook prints a line before and after each emit, and the diner prints a line for each dish. Before you read on, write down the order of the lines:

Java
// Java equivalent: Java has no Flow, so this is a hand-written push "flow".
// The cook calls the diner's Consumer once per dish.
static void cookDinner(List<String> card, Consumer<String> diner) {
    for (String dish : card) {
        System.out.println("cook    " + dish);
        diner.accept(dish);
        System.out.println("accept(" + dish + ") returned");
    }
}

cookDinner(card, dish -> System.out.println("eat     " + dish));
Kotlin
val dinner = flow {
    for (dish in card) {                     // "soup", "salad", "roast"
        println("cook    $dish")
        emit(dish)
        println("emit($dish) returned")
    }
}
println("flow built")
dinner.collect { dish -> println("eat     $dish") }
println("collect returned")

Two guesses are tempting. One says the three cook lines come first and then the three eat lines, as if emit put each dish on a shelf for later. The other gets the pairs right but prints emit(soup) returned before eat soup, as if emit handed the bowl over and walked off. Here is the real output:

flow built
cook    soup
eat     soup
emit(soup) returned
cook    salad
eat     salad
emit(salad) returned
cook    roast
eat     roast
emit(roast) returned
collect returned

flow built comes first, so building the flow ran none of its block. And eat soup comes before emit(soup) returned: the diner's code ran while emit was still running. The cook never put a plate down anywhere, because this kitchen has nowhere to put one. There is no queue here and no second thread, the worker that runs the code.

Flow basics gave you three rules about flows. They are cold, they handle one value at a time, and a slow collector slows the producer. All three come from one fact: emit is a plain function call into the collector.

The Java version prints the same order for the same reason. accept is a method call, and the line after a call runs when the call returns. About a dozen lines of Kotlin are enough to build a flow that works the same way, so let's write them.

sections.h: A flow from scratch: two interfaces and a three-line builder
sections.html:
A flow needs a receiving end and a sending end, and each one is a single suspend function. A suspend function is one that can pause without holding its thread, as the coroutines track showed from its first lesson. The piece of work that runs it is a coroutine, which can pause and carry on later. Here are the two ends, written from scratch, with toy names so they don't clash with the library's:

Java
// Java equivalent: the same two interfaces, with plain blocking methods
interface ToyCollector<T> {
    void emit(T value);
}

interface ToyFlow<T> {
    void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector);    // one abstract method, so a lambda is a ToyFlow
}
Kotlin
fun interface ToyCollector<in T> {
    suspend fun emit(value: T)
}

interface ToyFlow<out T> {
    suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>)
}

fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> =
    object : ToyFlow<T> {
        override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block()
    }

The first interface is the diner. A ToyCollector has one function, emit, that takes one value. The second is the recipe card. A ToyFlow has one function, collect, that takes a collector and pushes values into it. The in T and out T say which way values travel: a collector only takes values in, and a flow only hands them out.

The builder is the whole trick. toyFlow { ... } stores your block in an object and returns it. Nothing runs. When someone calls collect(collector), the object runs your block with that collector as its receiver, so this inside the block is the collector. Every emit(x) inside the block is really collector.emit(x): a direct call into the diner's code.

Let's use it like the real thing:

Java
ToyFlow<Integer> dishes = collector -> {
    for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) {
        System.out.println("  [producer] before emit(" + id + ")");
        collector.emit(id);
        System.out.println("  [producer] after emit(" + id + ")");
    }
};
System.out.println("built the flow, nothing ran yet");
dishes.collect(v -> System.out.println("  [collector] got " + v));
dishes.collect(v -> System.out.println("  [collector] got " + v));   // the block runs again
Kotlin
val dishes = toyFlow {
    for (id in 1..3) {
        println("  [producer] before emit($id)")
        emit(id)
        println("  [producer] after emit($id)")
    }
}
println("built the flow, nothing ran yet")
dishes.collect { v -> println("  [collector] got $v") }
dishes.collect { v -> println("  [collector] got $v") }   // the block runs again

Building prints nothing. The first collect runs the block, and each before emit(n) is followed by got n and only then by after emit(n). That's the pattern the dinner printed. The second collect runs the whole block again from the top. That is all cold means: a flow is a function you haven't called yet, and collect calls it. Two diners get two dinners, each cooked from the top.

The Java twin has the same shape and prints the same lines. What differs is the cost of waiting. Java's emit is an ordinary call, so while the diner eats, the cook's thread sits inside emit and can do nothing else. Kotlin's emit is a suspend call. If the diner calls delay or waits for a slow answer, the coroutine pauses and the thread goes off to run other coroutines. The order of events is the same in both.

The order matches. But "a direct call" is still my claim, and the call stack can settle it.

steps: Open ToyFlow.kt in the demo folder. It holds the two interfaces, the builder, a toy map and a main. Predict how many [producer] start lines it prints.
Run it. Check that built the flow, nothing ran yet comes before any producer line.
Add a third collection at the end of main: dishes.map { it + 1 }.map { it * 2 }.collect { println(it) }. Predict the values and the number of [producer] start lines, then run it.

code.title: ToyFlow.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking // A flow from scratch: two interfaces and a three-line builder. No kotlinx.coroutines flow types. // StackDemo.kt and Backpressure.kt in this folder use these too. fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } /** map is a collector wrapped in a collector. */ fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val dishes = toyFlow { println(" [producer] start") for (id in 1..3) { println(" [producer] before emit($id)") emit(id) println(" [producer] after emit($id)") } println(" [producer] done") } println("built the flow, nothing ran yet") println("--- first collect, through map") dishes.map { it * 100 }.collect { v -> println(" [collector] got $v") } println("--- second collect: the body runs again") dishes.collect { v -> println(" [collector] got $v") } }

alt.title: ToyFlowJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ToyFlow.kt: the same two interfaces, pushing values with a plain method call. // One difference: this emit blocks the thread while the collector works. In Kotlin emit is a // suspend call, so a collector that waits (delay, I/O) gives the thread back meanwhile. package workbench.flows.l01; import java.util.function.Function; public class ToyFlowJava { interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } // one abstract method, so Java takes a lambda for it interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); // map is a collector wrapped in a collector default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ToyFlow<Integer> dishes = collector -> { System.out.println(" [producer] start"); for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) { System.out.println(" [producer] before emit(" + id + ")"); collector.emit(id); System.out.println(" [producer] after emit(" + id + ")"); } System.out.println(" [producer] done"); }; System.out.println("built the flow, nothing ran yet"); System.out.println("--- first collect, through map"); dishes.map(id -> id * 100).collect(v -> System.out.println(" [collector] got " + v)); System.out.println("--- second collect: the body runs again"); dishes.collect(v -> System.out.println(" [collector] got " + v)); } }

try.expect: Two [producer] start lines, one per collect, and none before the built line. The first collection prints got 100, got 200 and got 300 through the toy map. Your third collection starts the block a third time and prints 4, 6 and 8: each value goes through both maps inside one emit call before the producer makes the next. The Java twin prints the same lines as the original Kotlin program.

sections.h: The diner runs inside emit: reading the stack
sections.html:
A call stack is the chain of method calls a thread is in the middle of, newest on top, and any thread can print its own. Let's print it from inside the diner:

Java
static void printStack(String label) {
    System.out.println(label + ", thread=" + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    StackTraceElement[] frames = Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace();
    for (int i = 2; i < frames.length; i++)
        System.out.println("    at " + frames[i].getClassName() + "." + frames[i].getMethodName());
}

ToyFlow<String> dinner = collector -> collector.emit("soup");
dinner.collect(value -> printStack("collector got " + value));
Kotlin
fun printStack(label: String) {
    println("$label, thread=${Thread.currentThread().name}")
    Thread.currentThread().stackTrace.drop(2)
        .takeWhile { !it.className.startsWith("kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask") }
        .forEach { println("    at ${it.className}.${it.methodName}") }
}

toyFlow { emit("soup") }.collect { printStack("collector got $it") }

For the toy flow it prints this. I trimmed the package names and the coroutine machinery at the bottom:

collector got soup, thread=main
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$2.emit             <- your collector lambda: the diner
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$2.emit
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invokeSuspend    <- the toyFlow { } block, calling emit
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invoke
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invoke
    at ToyFlowKt$toyFlow$1.collect           <- ToyFlow.collect, running the block
    at StackDemoKt$main$1.invokeSuspend      <- main, calling collect

Read it from the bottom. main called collect. collect ran the block. The block called emit, and emit is your lambda. It's all one thread, main. (Names such as $main$1$2 are classes the Kotlin compiler makes for lambdas, and invokeSuspend is where a suspend lambda's body runs.)

The real flow { }.map { } gives a taller stack with the same shape. Here I also dropped repeated frames and two helper frames:

collector got SOUP, thread=main
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$5.emit                                   <- your lambda
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$invokeSuspend$$inlined$map$1$2.emit      <- map's collector
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.SafeCollector.emit         <- a checker
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$3.invokeSuspend                          <- your flow { } block
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SafeFlow.collectSafely
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.AbstractFlow.collect
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$invokeSuspend$$inlined$map$1.collect     <- map's collect
    at StackDemoKt$main$1.invokeSuspend                            <- main

map is an operator, a function that takes a flow and returns a new one, here a flow that changes each value. It's also an inline function: the compiler copies its body into the calling code, so its collector shows up as a class in your own file. SafeCollector is a checker that flow { } puts in front of your collector. Lesson 2 of this track opens it up.

Here is the picture to keep. In the coroutines track the cook stood for a thread. Here she stands for the producer, and emit is her walk to the table: she carries one plate over and stands there while the diner eats. Only when the diner is done does she walk back and plate the next one. A map is a helper who stands between them, adds the sauce, carries the plate on and waits at the table too. In the stack, each of them is a box inside the one before.

The picture breaks at the waiting. A real cook standing at the table is lost to the kitchen. A suspended coroutine holds no thread: while your diner is inside delay or waiting for a slow answer, the thread runs other coroutines, and only this one dinner is held up.

A plain flow is one call stack. The collector runs inside emit.

So the call shape is real. Next, the three rules from Flow basics fall straight out of it.

sections.h: Cold, one at a time, and slowed by the diner: three rules from one call
sections.html:
The rules you learned about flows all follow from that stack.

A flow is cold because the block is the body of collect. No collect, no run. Two collect calls, two runs.

A flow is sequential, one value at a time, because emit can't return before the collector's code returns. The cook can't start the salad while the soup is still being eaten, and within one collection the diner never holds two plates at once. That's also why the KDoc of FlowCollector (KDoc is the documentation written in Kotlin source, like Javadoc) says emit "is not thread-safe and should not be invoked concurrently". FlowCollector is the library's version of our toy collector, and a plain call has nothing that would protect it from two callers at once.

A flow also gets backpressure for free. Backpressure means a slow consumer slows the producer down, so values don't pile up in memory. Reactive Streams, the standard behind the Reactor library from the reactive track, needs a whole protocol of requests for that. A flow needs nothing, because the cook is stuck inside emit until the diner is done.

Let's put numbers on it. The cook needs 100 ms per dish and the diner 300 ms to eat it. The demo runs under runTest, which uses virtual time: a fake clock from the coroutines test library, where delay moves the clock forward at once. So the numbers are exact and the run takes no real time. Both the toy and the real flow { } print:

t= 100 emit 1
t= 400 eaten  1     <- emit(1) returns only now
t= 500 emit 2       <- 100 + 300 + 100
t= 800 eaten  2
t= 900 emit 3
t=1200 eaten  3     <- (100 + 300) x 3

The second emit happens at t=500, and it can't happen earlier: from 100 to 400 the cook was inside emit(1), standing at the table. That's the warm-up question.

Free backpressure isn't fast backpressure. Three dishes took 1,200 ms, where the slower side alone needs only 900. A shelf between the kitchen and the table would let the cook work while the diner eats. Lesson 4 of this track adds one, called a buffer, and pays for it in memory.

In a plain flow the times add up: each value costs the producer's time plus the collector's.

Stopping early goes through the same call. A collector that wants no more values, like the one behind take(2), has no handle on the cook's loop. All it can do is throw an exception. The exception flies back up through emit, the cook's loop ends, and her finally blocks run on the way out. The real take does exactly this with a special exception, which the next lesson takes apart. You'll write the toy version in the lab.

So the toy and the real thing behave alike, down to the millisecond. How close is the toy to the library's own interfaces?

code.title: Backpressure.kt
code.html: @file:OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) package workbench.flows.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // A cook who needs 100 ms to cook each dish and a diner who needs 300 ms to eat it. // runTest runs on virtual time: delay() moves a fake clock, so the numbers are exact and the // program finishes at once. fun main() = runTest { val t = { testScheduler.currentTime } println("=== the toy flow") toyFlow { for (id in 1..3) { delay(100) println(" t=%4d emit %d".format(t(), id)) emit(id) } }.collect { id -> delay(300) println(" t=%4d eaten %d".format(t(), id)) } val toyEnd = t() println(" total ${toyEnd} ms") println("=== kotlinx flow { }") flow { for (id in 1..3) { delay(100) println(" t=%4d emit %d".format(t() - toyEnd, id)) emit(id) } }.collect { id -> delay(300) println(" t=%4d eaten %d".format(t() - toyEnd, id)) } println(" total ${t() - toyEnd} ms") }

alt.title: BackpressureJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of Backpressure.kt: the hand-written push flow with Thread.sleep in real time. // The cook needs 100 ms per dish, the diner 300 ms to eat it. Here the thread is // blocked during both sleeps; in Kotlin's delay it would be free for other coroutines. package workbench.flows.l01; public class BackpressureJava { interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.currentTimeMillis(); ToyFlow<Integer> dishes = collector -> { for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) { sleep(100); System.out.printf(" t=%4d emit %d%n", System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, id); collector.emit(id); } }; dishes.collect(id -> { sleep(300); System.out.printf(" t=%4d eaten %d%n", System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, id); }); System.out.printf(" total %d ms (real time, so a little more than 1200)%n", System.currentTimeMillis() - t0); } }

try.expect: emit 3 at t=900 and a total of 1200 ms, the same for both flows. With a 50 ms diner, emit 2 is at t=250 (100 + 50 + 100) and the total is 450 ms, three rounds of 150. The Java run shows the same pattern in real time, with every number a little late. On this busy machine the first eaten line came about 70 ms late and the total was 1277 ms, because real sleeps overshoot and a cold JVM is slow at its first prints.

video.title: The collector runs inside emit, so the cook waits at the table: a flow handles one value at a time, and with a 100 ms reader and a 300 ms collector the second emit comes at 500 ms, not 200

sections.h: The real Flow, and operators as collectors inside collectors
sections.html:
Very close. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0, the coroutines library this course uses, the two interfaces are:

Java
// Java equivalent: java.util.concurrent.Flow, the JDK's Reactive Streams interfaces (abridged)
interface Publisher<T>  { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> subscriber); }
interface Subscription  { void request(long n); void cancel(); }
interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription subscription);
    void onNext(T item);
    void onError(Throwable throwable);
    void onComplete();
}
Kotlin
public interface Flow<out T> {
    public suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>)
}

public fun interface FlowCollector<in T> {
    public suspend fun emit(value: T)
}

Only FlowCollector is a fun interface, an interface with one abstract method that a lambda can be turned into. That's how flow.collect { v -> ... } takes your lambda: Kotlin converts the lambda into a FlowCollector. Flow is a plain interface, so Flow { ... } doesn't compile ("interface ... does not have constructors"). That's on purpose. Its KDoc says Flow "is not stable for inheritance in 3rd party libraries", because new methods may be added to it later. Build flows with flow { }, or extend AbstractFlow, which is marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi.

Java's own java.util.concurrent.Flow, in the JDK since Java 9, works the other way round. The subscriber pulls: it calls request(n), and the publisher may send at most n more items. Kotlin's flow needs no such call, because the cook can't get ahead of a call that hasn't returned yet.

Operators are flows built on flows. Here is map on the toy:

Java
// a default method in the Java ToyFlow interface
default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) {
    return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value)));
}
Kotlin
fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> =
    toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } }

Read it from the inside out. map returns a new flow. When that flow is collected, it collects the flow above it with a collector of its own, and that collector calls the next emit with the new value. It's a collector wrapped in a collector: the helper who takes each plate from the cook, adds the sauce and carries it on. filter is the same thing with an if around the emit, a helper who only passes on the plates that pass a check. The library writes both in nearly the same way, as the next lesson shows.

So a chain of five operators is five nested calls for each value. That's why the stack grew by one emit frame per map, and why operators need no locks or queues between them. This shape also names the parts of a chain. Everything above an operator, towards the cook, is its upstream. Everything below it, towards the diner, is its downstream.

The toy is honest, but it's also trusting. Nothing stops a toy flow from calling emit from another thread, or from carrying on after the diner sent a plate back. The real flow { } checks for both, and that's where we go next.

compare.title: The toy flow in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ToyFlowJava.java (abridged)
java.html: // Java equivalent: a hand-written push flow. emit blocks the thread while the collector works. interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } ToyFlow<Integer> dishes = collector -> { for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) collector.emit(id); }; dishes.map(id -> id * 100).collect(v -> System.out.println("got " + v));

kotlin.title: ToyFlow.kt (abridged)
kotlin.html: fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } val dishes = toyFlow { for (id in 1..3) emit(id) } dishes.map { it * 100 }.collect { v -> println("got $v") }

compare.note: Both versions have the same two interfaces and the same map, and the calls happen in the same order. What differs is underneath. Java's emit blocks a thread while the collector works, so a thousand slow collections need a thousand threads. Kotlin's emit suspends a coroutine, and the thread is free during the wait. Java lets any interface with one abstract method take a lambda, so a lambda can be a ToyFlow. Kotlin asks for fun interface, and the real Flow leaves it out on purpose, which is why you build flows through flow { }. Kotlin also declares variance on the interfaces (out T on the flow, in T on the collector), where Java would write ? super T at every use.

worked.title: Write a toy operator that times the downstream

steps.say: The cook wants to know how long each dish takes, so she wraps a timer around emit. It says 300 ms per dish, and she starts looking for a faster stove. Before she buys one, write a toy operator that measures exactly what a timer around emit measures. It has the shape of map: collect the flow above, and wrap the call to the next emit.
steps.code: fun <T> ToyFlow<T>.timeDownstream(record: (value: T, took: Duration) -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = toyFlow { this@timeDownstream.collect { value -> val mark = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow() // 1. start the clock emit(value) // 2. every operator below, and the collector record(value, mark.elapsedNow()) // 3. stop it when the downstream returns } }

alt.html: // a default method in the Java ToyFlow interface default ToyFlow<T> timeDownstream(BiConsumer<T, Long> record) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> { long start = System.nanoTime(); // 1. start the clock downstream.emit(value); // 2. everything below runs here record.accept(value, (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); // 3. stop it, in ms }); }

steps.say: Put it between a cook who needs 100 ms per dish and a diner who needs 300 ms to eat. In real time it prints about 300 ms for every dish. That's the diner's time. The cook's own 100 ms happens before emit and never shows up, so the stove was never the problem.
steps.code: toyFlow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit("dish-$i") } } // the cook .timeDownstream { dish, took -> println("$dish downstream took ${took.inWholeMilliseconds} ms") } .collect { delay(300) } // the diner // dish-1 downstream took 300 ms (give or take a few, in real time)

alt.html: ToyFlow<String> cook = collector -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { sleep(100); collector.emit("dish-" + i); } // the cook }; cook.timeDownstream((dish, ms) -> System.out.println(dish + " downstream took " + ms + " ms")) .collect(dish -> sleep(300)); // the diner

steps.say: Where you put it decides what it measures. Each operator in a plain flow sees, inside its emit, the time of everything below it. So moving the timer down the chain takes operators out of the number.
steps.code: cook.map { plate(it) }.timeDownstream(log).collect { diner.eat(it) } // the diner only cook.timeDownstream(log).map { plate(it) }.collect { diner.eat(it) } // plating plus the diner

alt.html: cook.map(d -> plate(d)).timeDownstream(log).collect(diner::eat); // the diner only cook.timeDownstream(log).map(d -> plate(d)).collect(diner::eat); // plating plus the diner

steps.say: The library's onEach has the same shape with your action in front of emit. In its source it is transform { value -> action(value); return@transform emit(value) }. On the toy it is one line:
steps.code: fun <T> ToyFlow<T>.onEach(action: suspend (T) -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = toyFlow { this@onEach.collect { value -> action(value); emit(value) } }

alt.html: default ToyFlow<T> onEach(Consumer<T> action) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> { action.accept(value); downstream.emit(value); }); }

lab.title: Build the toy flow and make take stop the producer
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. Read the test names in ToyFlowTest: they are the spec.
Write toyFlow and toList. Three tests turn green: running the block again, the event order, and the slow collector in virtual time.
Write map and filter as collectors wrapped in collectors. Don't collect into a list first. The event-order test checks that each value goes all the way down before the producer makes the next one.

Write take. Check count with require before you build the flow. Inside, make a fresh Any() as your marker, emit each value, and after the count-th one throw ToyAbortException(marker). Catch it around the upstream collect, and rethrow it if e.owner !== marker.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them once more.
hints: take can't return from the producer's loop, because that loop is someone else's code. Throwing from the collector is the only way out. The exception travels back through the producer's emit, which is why the producer's finally runs.
Compare markers with !==, which tests identity. Two Any() objects are never the same object, and that is the point of the marker: it's the name signed on the note.

If the nested-take test fails and your result has an extra 99 in it, your take catches every ToyAbortException. The inner take(3) swallowed the outer take(1)'s abort, so the outer block carried on and emitted 99.
Put require(count > 0) before return toyFlow { ... }, so a bad count fails when the flow is built, as it does for the library's take.

drill.title: Write the two interfaces from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In a blank file, write ToyCollector, ToyFlow, the toyFlow builder and map, with no imports from kotlinx.coroutines.flow. Then write two lines that prove the flow is cold. Check the variance: which interface gets out T, and which gets in T?

answer.html: fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { // it only takes values in suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { // it only hands values out suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } // cold: building prints nothing, each collect prints "run" again val f = toyFlow { println("run"); emit(1) } runBlocking { f.collect { }; f.collect { } } // run, run

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same shape with plain methods (no variance on the declarations) interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } // cold: building prints nothing, each collect prints "run" again ToyFlow<Integer> f = c -> { System.out.println("run"); c.emit(1); }; f.collect(v -> { }); f.collect(v -> { }); // run, run

recap: A flow is two interfaces with one suspend function each: Flow.collect(collector) and FlowCollector.emit(value).
flow { } only stores your block, like a recipe card. collect runs it, from the top, once per call. That is what cold means.
emit is a direct call into the collector. The collector's code runs inside emit, on the same stack and the same thread: the cook stands at the table while the diner eats.
So a plain flow handles one value at a time, and a slow collector slows the producer. With 100 ms and 300 ms per item, the second emit is at t=500.
Operators like map and filter are collectors wrapped in collectors. A collector stops the producer by throwing back up through emit, so the producer's finally runs.

The limit: the times add up (1,200 ms where the slower side alone needs 900), and the toy checks nothing at all. Lesson 2 shows the checks in flow { }; lesson 4 adds a shelf so the cook can work ahead.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "My flow cooks in the background and keeps the dishes on a shelf until the diner catches up." Explain, from the call shape, what really happens in a plain flow.
explain.answer: A plain flow has no background work and no shelf. flow { } only stores the cook's code, and collect runs it in the collector's own coroutine. Each emit(dish) is a direct call into the collector's code, so the diner eats while the cook is still inside emit. Only when the collector returns does emit return, and only then does the cook make the next dish. So the cook is never more than one dish ahead, it all runs on the same thread, and a slow diner slows the cook down. If we want the cook to work ahead, we have to ask for it with an operator such as buffer or flowOn, and those add a second coroutine and a channel between the two sides.

deeper.html:
A few details help when you read real stack traces and real code.

Line numbers in inlined frames can mislead. map is inline, so its collector's code is copied into your file, and the frame's file and line point into the library source it came from. They can even point past the end of that file. In one run, map's frame pointed at Emitters.kt:217. Trust the class name ($$inlined$map$1$2) more than the line.

flow.collect { } calls the member function Flow.collect, with your lambda converted into a FlowCollector. Older versions had an inline extension collect(action). It is still in 1.11.0, but marked @Deprecated(level = DeprecationLevel.HIDDEN) for JS and Native compatibility, so your code never calls it. In a stack trace your lambda appears as a generated class's emit method.

You can implement Flow yourself with object : Flow<T>. It compiles, and it behaves like the toy, with no checks at all. That's the reason not to. A hand-written Flow can call emit from another thread, or keep emitting after the collector failed, and nothing stops it. The next lesson shows the checks flow { } runs on every emit, and what goes wrong without them.

java.util.concurrent.Flow (JDK 9 and later) is the JDK's copy of the Reactive Streams interfaces. Its contract has rules a Kotlin flow gets from the call shape: a publisher must not send more items than were requested, and it must not call onNext from two threads at once. In a plain Kotlin flow the first rule is replaced by emit not returning, and the second holds because there is only one call at a time.
